transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-08-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 78 mins
Attendees: Alex (AE), Priya (SE), Jon (Solutions Eng) - Redwood; Mike (Platform), Sara (Security), Arjun (SRE), Lena (Prod ML) - Nimbus

Summary: quick infra recap, deep dive on PrivateLink stitching between Nimbus VPC and Redwood private endpoints, NAT/hairpinning impacts, DNS resolver selection and TTL behavior, KV cache consistency across multi-az, batching tradeoffs and quantization guidance for their 2k token chat workload. Agreed next steps to run a hands-on lab and exchange runbooks.

Topics: PrivateLink topology, route tables, cross-account ENIs, NAT gateway egress and hairpinning, resolver pathing, MTU fragmentation, KV cache warmup & cache miss penalties, batching latency vs throughput curves, int8 quantization CPU fallbacks.

[00:00] Alex: ok thanks everyone for joining, um we'll try to respect the 78 minutes, high level we're focused on the PrivateLink stitching questions you sent in the doc and then run through KV cache implications for your mixed short/long context workload
[00:22] Mike: thanks Alex, yeah our main pain is spikes in per-token latency during traffic bursts and sometimes long tail 500ms outliers when requests hit cold k-v caches, and we also have strict data residency so hosted isn't an option, we need private vpc or dedicated
[00:48] Priya: got it, when you say cold KV cache are you seeing cache misses on the same host or cross-host evictions?
[00:55] Mike: a mix, Arjun can maybe chime in the eviction seems correlated with autoscaling events and also when traffic is routed through a different AZ after a failover
[01:08] Arjun: yeah we saw the worker pools rebalanced and keys got dropped, also when traffic hairpins through the NAT path we saw increased RTTs, sometimes packet fragmentation due to MTU mismatch on the interconnects
[01:24] Jon: hmm MTU issues are classic with cross-account privatelink peering and some transit GW setups, are you using jumbo frames anywhere or forced 1500?
[01:33] Arjun: everything's 1500 on our side, but the partner DC side is 9000 for internal, so when the path includes their edge it fragments
[01:42] Priya: that fragmentation can add tens of ms in tail latency, and also impacts our continuous batching. The runtime keeps waiting on the last bytes for a token batch boundary, which amplifies latency variance
[01:55] Lena: one thing we observed is that when we increase batch size to 16 we get better throughput but the P95 goes up from ~80ms to ~220ms for short queries, is that expected?
[02:08] Priya: yep that's the classic latency vs throughput trade off — continuous batching helps amortize kernel launch and KV cache lookups, but for short tail queries single-request-mode or smaller batching keeps P95 lower. We typically recommend adaptive batching for mixed workloads
[02:25] Sara: on the security side we need to ensure PrivateLink endpoints are cross-account with least-priv IAM, and also full audit logs going to our SIEM. Does Redwood support envelope encryption with our KMS?
[02:36] Alex: yes you can bring-your-own-KMS, we support HSM-backed keys for private deployments. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the runbook link: https://docs.redwood.com/privatelink-runbook (note: this is a reference)
[02:50] Mike: great. Back to the KV cache, is the cache local to the GPU worker or shared via a sidecar? We run multi-tenant pools and want to avoid noisy neighbor evictions
[03:03] Priya: the Redwood runtime uses per-worker KV caches in GPU memory with a small shared LRU in host memory for fast warmup. On Dedicated you can pin model shards to GPUs to reduce cross-host cache misses; on Private VPC we can provision reserved pools too
[03:17] Mike: when you say host memory LRU are we talking about a second-level cache that can be persisted across restarts?
[03:23] Priya: it's in RAM, ephemeral; we recommend sticky sessions or session affinity at the load balancer to maximize cache hit rates for long chat sessions
[03:33] Arjun: sticky sessions sounds risky for our autoscaling goals though, we prefer stateless workers and rely on KV replication, is that viable?
[03:44] Jon: we do have an optional KV replication service across AZs but it trades write amplification and complexity; for most workloads sticky sessions + warmup heuristics work best for latency SLOs
[03:56] [04:00] Mike: ok, can we talk through the PrivateLink routing? We want cross-account privatelink from our VPC to Redwood's ingestion endpoints in the customer's region, but also need egress to our internal services (metrics, secrets) through the NAT. How do you recommend avoiding hairpin / double-NAT?
[04:20] Priya: the recommended pattern is to provision an interface endpoint in your VPC that points to the Redwood service endpoint (cross-account). Route tables for subnets with workers should prefer the endpoint for 10.x/100.x host ranges. For internal egress, we recommend using a dedicated egress-only NAT or egress VPC with route propagation so traffic to your internal IP ranges doesn't flow back through the privatelink path
[04:43] Sara: and DNS resolution — do we resolve the privatelink alias via our resolver? We had an issue where our recursive resolver returned public IPs and the connection went out over the internet briefly
[04:56] Alex: yes that happens if the resolver isn't doing conditional forwarding. You need to set the VPC resolver rules to prefer the service domain to the privatelink endpoint. Also watch TTLs — cached public answers can linger for a few minutes and break the cutover during failovers
[05:12] Arjun: is there a recommended TTL for quick failovers? We need fast failover between AZs with minimal cold-cache hits
[05:21] Priya: 30s-60s can be aggressive but helps. Combine that with a small health-check-based client-side fallback that retries to a secondary endpoint while preserving session tokens, that reduces user-visible errors during DNS propagation windows
[05:36] Mike: we ran a lab where DNS propagation caused a 2 min blackhole while endpoints rotated, caused large cache misses
[05:45] Priya: yep that blackhole is painful. Our suggestion: coordinate canary cutovers, drain connections, pre-warm KV caches by replaying recent sessions to the new pool; we provided a pre-warm script in the repo last year — we'll link that
[05:58] Jon: note that pre-warm increases token cost during cutover, but it beats a degraded P95 for customers
[06:05] Lena: about quantization — we want to try int8 to reduce GPU memory footprint, but we're worried about occasional accuracy regressions on our retrieval-augmented prompts. What's Redwood's stance?
[06:17] Priya: we have quantization profiles per model class. int8 can be 'mostly transparent' for generation but some tasks like reranking or logit-sensitive tasks see regressions. We recommend a staged approach: quantize a clone of the model, run model evals on a prompt set, and monitor quality regressions with metrics like token-level perplexity delta and behavioral tests
[06:35] Arjun: what's the perf boost typically? For our T4-like footprints we expect 2-3x memory reduction and some speedup depending on kernel support
[06:44] Priya: yes memory reduction is real; latency improvements can be model and kernel dependent — on Ampere GPUs you often see 10-30% token throughput improvement, on older hardware the inference path might actually get slightly slower if kernel fallback triggers
[06:59] [07:05] Mike: any gotchas with quantization + KV cache? We saw cases where KV cache token encoding differed and the cache missed because of floating point rounding differences after quantization
[07:16] Priya: that can happen if you change tokenizer pre/post-processing or if you change key encoding. Our runtime tags KV keys by model version + quantization profile so a mismatch won't reuse the wrong cache entries. But during transitions you'll get inevitable cold-cache penalties. Best practice: run a canary traffic split with pinned sessions and a small percent of requests to the quantized variant while warming its cache
[07:36] Sara: compliance question — are audit logs for cache evictions captured? We need to show proof the cache never leaks PII across tenants
[07:45] Alex: eviction traces and per-token lineage can be captured to your log sink; for private deployments we can forward memcache telemetry to your SIEM and redact token text, we do token-level hashes for lineage
[07:58] Arjun: can you expand on sticky sessions vs shared KV replication costs? We're trying to budget for committed capacity and want predictable billing
[08:12] Priya: sticky sessions reduce compute throughput efficiency but give lower tail latency and fewer cross-host transfers. Replication increases network egress and storage costs. If you commit to reserved Dedicated pools you can get predictable units and then tune batch sizes to hit throughput targets while preserving latency SLOs
[08:30] Mike: QC question — our client uses a managed egress proxy cluster for outbound calls (metrics, secrets agent). We worry about hairpin where privatelink traffic goes to endpoint and then back out through the egress proxy — any routing patterns to avoid that?
[08:44] Jon: yes, you can add policy-based routing: route 10.x service CIDR to the interface endpoint, and set a more specific route for your egress proxy CIDR to the NAT/egress VPC. Also, keep the endpoint subnets separate from egress subnets
[08:58] [09:05] Lena: let's talk benchmarks — Priya, can you outline the benchmark script you'll run in the lab? We want end-to-end P50/P95/P99, token-per-second throughput, and cold vs warm KV hit scenarios
[09:20] Priya: sure, script overview: 1) synthetic load generator that replays 1k recent chat sessions with realistic turn lengths, 2) step load from 50rps to 500rps to capture autoscale events, 3) record per-request KV hit/miss, kernel time, network RTT to endpoint, and per-token latency, 4) run quantized variant after baseline with same seed prompts. We'll provide output CSVs and heatmap dashboards.
[09:45] Mike: will the script reproduce the NAT hairpin scenario? We want to test their egress path re-write
[09:51] Priya: yes, we'll include an option to force egress via your NAT to simulate hairpin and show delta in the heatmaps
[09:58] Arjun: how long does a realistic warmup take to bring KV hit rates to acceptable levels for large chat flows? We saw needing 30-45 minutes previously
[10:07] Priya: depends on your session distribution; with sticky sessions and pre-warm replay, under 15 minutes for hot keys; if your user pool has long tail cold sessions expect longer. We'll measure cache warming half-life in the lab and provide a recommended warmup cadence
[10:22] Sara: security: we need SAML SSO and RBAC scoped by team, plus immutable audit trails. Any limitations in private deployment?
[10:31] Alex: we support enterprise SAML and fine-grained RBAC on the console. For Private, the control plane can be customer-managed in VPC and audit logs are shipped to your audit sink. We'll share the compliance appendix
[10:42] Mike: one more network question — we're using transit GW with multiple account VPCs, will privatelink to Redwood endpoint keep traffic inside the region or will it bounce to the transit gateway?
[10:52] Priya: interface endpoints are regional and traffic goes directly to the service endpoint within the region. Transit GW interactions get tricky if you have centralised egress; we recommend local egress for inference subnets to keep latency low
[11:04] Jon: also monitor ENI limits per AZ for interface endpoints; low ENI quotas can cause late failures under scale, we've seen customers cap out on small accounts
[11:15] Arjun: good call, we'll check our limits.
[11:20] [11:30] Alex: ok let's sketch an action plan — we'll run the benchmark with: baseline hosted-in-privatelink, quantized canary, hairpin mode. We'll produce a heatmap of per-packet RTT vs per-token latency and KV miss distribution. Any other metrics?
[11:40] Mike: please include connection churn, ENI attach/detach events, and DNS TTL expirations in the timeline
[11:46] Priya: noted, we'll include them in the timeline CSV. We'll also give you the pre-warm script and an example CloudFormation to create endpoints and route rules
[11:56] Sara: one administrative — we need a non-prod SOC2 checklist for the pilot to show auditors, can you provide that?
[12:05] Alex: yes we'll attach a pilot scope checklist with required controls and evidence types
[12:11] [12:20] Mike: small nit: when we tried PrivateLink last month we saw TLS SNI mismatch with our mutual TLS proxy, any tips?
[12:27] Jon: check that the endpoint's CN/SNI are set to the Redwood service domain and that your proxy isn't re-writing host headers. With mTLS you also need to ensure certificate chains are trusted by the endpoint
[12:37] Priya: for canary cutover we recommend running a dual-write for metrics to avoid blind spots and maintain parity between old and new pools
[12:46] Alex: ok wrapping up — recap of next steps, action items we logged, we'll set up the hands-on lab next Wed/Thu, exchange runbook and scripts.

Transcript notes: occasional speaker mislabels (Speaker 1 shows up in the middle), minor transcription errors e.g., 'k v' vs 'KV', 'privatelink' vs 'private link', punctuation and filler words preserved. References shared: https://docs.redwood.com/privatelink-runbook (topology + KMS), https://github.com/redwood/benchmarks (benchmark scripts), and a sample CloudFormation snippet to create interface endpoints.

End of transcript.
